utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, my colleague Ann Sutherland, and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Defence is Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Eaoadin O'Brien, Novak Lukic, lead counsel, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Treanor, I know you will know this, but it's still the duty of the Bench to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I wish to take you back to something you said at the very end of the court session on Tuesday, which appears at page 1035 of the transcript. There you were discussing the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You were describing the results of the November 1990 elections and the number of seats won in the two houses of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly by the different groups. You stated on lines 4 to 9 and, I will quote: "The Party for Democratic Action, which was basically a Muslim party, won 80-odd seats, and the HDZ in Croatia won a smaller number of seats. Each of those parties won a number of seats in the Assembly roughly proportionate to the representation of the respective nationalities in the population of BH." Did you mean the HDZ in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant the HDZ in BH. Perhaps this might be a good time for me to correct a couple of other errors I made in my testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I believe that if there are errors to be corrected, it is appropriate that counsel appoint the witness to where he needs to go, as opposed to the witness independently determining what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what were the issues that concern you in relation to your testimony on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two points, perhaps minor, but just so the record is straight --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me once again. I believe that we may be having a transfer of function here. As I understand it, Ms. Sutherland is the attorney; Mr. Treanor is the witness. If Ms. Sutherland, representing the Prosecution, has concerns about the state of her record, then she should direct the witness to how to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Treanor should be given the opportunity to correct anything on the record that he, on reflection, has a problem with that he told you. We are here for the establishment of the truth, not for the fact that he may have said something incorrectly on Tuesday and is now not allowed to correct himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's a problem that's being posed here, Your Honour, which is, as I understand it, there is to be no communication as between the attorney and the witness during their testimony. Obviously, what that would mean, then, is that the attorney, after reviewing the record, has made a determination that there are some difficulties, either mistakes, errors, or something incorrect. Obviously that's not the state of play that we have here, which would cause me some great concern, and I think I'll address that a little bit later. But once again, if the attorney has some concerns - and I have absolutely no difficulty with the assertion made that we're here to seek the truth and find out what happened - if the attorney believes that those difficulties exist, then they should lead or direct the witness to where those difficulties are. Clearly, something else has happened here, and to the extent that something else has happened here, I can address that right now, but that's really a secondary issue to the -- my initial objection. The secondary issue being that apparently there's been conversation as between the witness and the representative of the OTP, which, as I understand it, should not have occurred. He said he understood the admonition. Apparently the admonition has been violated. The extent to which it's been violated, I do not know, and the extent to which we would need to -- or the Chamber may wish to inquire as to the nature, manner, of discussion, time of discussion, whether or not the discussion dealt with -- well, I won't define what it could have dealt with, as a matter of fact, and perhaps it would be more appropriate for the witness to leave the room at this point if that's the case. But in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have made a very serious accusation against the professional conduct of your opposite number. May I find out from you what the basis for that allegation is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- from what has transpired now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. We began the proceedings today with the following -- with the following -- with the following, which is a correction concerning the issue of where seats were won. Excuse me. Thereafter, Mr. Treanor says: "Perhaps this might be a good time for me to correct other errors I made in my testimony," at which point I direct my objection in the way that I did. And Ms. Sutherland -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, what happened now we are all aware of. Just tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based upon what happened now, I was -- I am led to believe that there's been contact between the OTP and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you infer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By virtue of the -- of the question asked and the answers given. Now, perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So perhaps the best -- the best starting point as opposed to the strength of my objection, in the event that I am wrong because if I am wrong I certainly don't wish to offend, is to make a determination, if the Chamber feels it appropriate, as to whether or not there's been any communication as between the two parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is I don't understand the logic of your argument, but before I express how I interpret this, I would like Madam Sutherland to give an answer, if she has any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not laid eyes on Mr. Treanor, much less spoken to him, since he began his testimony on Monday. Apart from seeing him in the courtroom, I have not spoken to Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I stand corrected, and I apologise to Ms. Sutherland personally, and I apologise to the Court for raising the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to make -- give you an analysis because I've been asking you for the basis of your allegation, and I want to tell you -- to give you the basis for my view that Madam Sutherland is right. Madam Sutherland stood up here and asked a question that was supposed to correct about the issue of the seats won. So far as she had re-read or read the transcript, that's what she felt needed correction. She hadn't -- she didn't ask the next question. But the witness then says, Maybe this will be an opportunity for me to correct other mistakes that I made in my past testimony. He says this from his own recollection of what he said on Friday and what he recalls as being the true state of affairs in relation to what he said, and that is why Madam Sutherland -- when you object, Madam Sutherland says, Yes, Witness, what is the thing you have concerns about, because she doesn't know. And why doesn't she know? Because she has not talked to him. Now, I don't see how, from that interaction, anybody can infer that there had been a communication between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the mind is -- the mind is a curious thing, and that's where my mind went. I obviously was mistaken. I recognise the mistake that I've made and, as I said before and as I will say again, to the extent that I engage in an illogical thought process, which on occasion I think occurs with me and certainly with others, but certainly with me, I apologise both to the Chamber and to Ms. Sutherland because I certainly don't want to be in a position where illogic, as opposed to logic, takes hold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, the objection is overruled. You're allowed to ask the witness to tell us what it is he wants to correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two issues in relation to events in early 1991. First of all, the meeting known as the Convention for Yugoslavia that took place on the 3rd of January in Belgrade took place in the building of the federal assembly and not in the other building that I may have mentioned. Another matter relates to the sequence of decisions relating to the referendums in Croatia. I think I misstated one date at least. The sequence is as follows: On the 21st of February, 1991, the Croatian Sabor passed the resolution on the procedure for the dissolution of Yugoslavia that I mentioned and also passed an amendment to the constitutional law which, in effect, invalidated federal law within Croatia. One week later, on the 28th of February, 1992, the Serbian National Council in Croatia passed its resolution, in effect, denying the validity of Croatian law in the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. Then on the 1st of April, 1992, came the decision that we saw, briefly at least, relating to the scheduling of a referendum in the Serbian Autonomous District, and it was then only on the 25th of April, 1992, that the Croatian Sabor passed its resolution on holding a referendum in the whole of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm unclear as to the second date. Do I understand that to be that of the 25th of April, which is reflected on page 8, line 1, as a date correction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the correct date. I'm going by memory. Again, I think, yesterday I may have said the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I was at a loss as to what was being corrected because it's a very long paragraph, and if the date just relates to the date of the 25th of April, thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have misstated the date of the 21st of February as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, on the transcript before you, at line 8, you -- it says: "Only then on the 25th of April, 1992, the Croatian Sabor passed a resolution ..." Did you in fact mean --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I have Rule 65 ter number 02232 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 02232, pages 2 to 4 of the English and pages 4, 6, and 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you finished testifying on Tuesday by telling the Chamber of the number of seats won for the two houses in the Bosnian Serb -- Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly. Can we move now to February 1991. What was the Bosnian Serb view, re staying in one Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time the Serbian democratic representatives in the new Assembly in the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina still wished to remain within Yugoslavia. At this time they were facing an attempt by the SDA deputies in the Assembly to introduce a resolution on the independence and sovereignty of BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did they express this view publicly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They issued a document entitled "The Views and Positions on the Future of Bosnia and Herzegovina" which stated their position on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did Mr. Izetbegovic, the President of the SDA, reveal the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's position in relation to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- as I mentioned, in this document, the Serbian Democratic Party set out its position. The next month, in March 1991, there was a meeting of the Presidents of the republics of the former Yugoslavia to discuss the future of the country and Mr. Izetbegovic made a certain statement after that meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if you can just pause there --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which related to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I seek to tender Rule 65 ter number 02232 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter number 02232 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May the Registrar call up 65 ter number 06784, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if you can continue. You were -- you stated that Mr. Izetbegovic issued a statement.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after the meeting in question on the 28th of March, 1991, through the discussions among the Presidents of the republics in which the issue of federation versus confederation figured, Mr. Izetbegovic made a statement which is quoted or cited in the press. I think it's at the end of -- the very end of this document, which is in English, and I will read it: "Bosnia-Herzegovina President Alija Izetbegovic announced that the republican parliament will soon adopt a declaration on the republic's independence even against the will of the Serbian Democratic Party, the second strongest party in the republican parliament. Similar declarations have already been adopted --" it says adapted, should be "adopted by the republics of Croatia, Macedonia, and Slovenia."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might. The document itself, as I have it, reads: "... would soon adopt a declaration of the republic's independence" as opposed to "on the republic's independence."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I could be directed to the paragraph that is being read because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page we've got a paragraph that is incomplete. It's not completely visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Actually, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It says: "President Tudjman reiterated he still does not rule out the need for a possible internationalisation of the Yugoslav question, particularly due to the situation in the Knin region."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I might be of some assistance, Your Honour. It's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not on the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When I saw the half -- the unfull paragraph, I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Treanor to ask the Registrar to take the page down, thinking it was at the bottom of the page, but it's, in fact, on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but even right down, there was nothing on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you meant -- you were referring to the last paragraph of this document, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May that document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sutherland --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might with regard to the last document, I note that part of the document has been redacted. I don't know the purpose of that, and I am not ascribing anything to that, the redaction itself. However, it was my understanding that this was, I believe, a public-source document that was from the witness's testimony, a document regarding that was stated in the press. If I'm correct in that manner, I don't understand specifically why we have redactions here. So if we just have some clarification about that, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document, as we can see from -- if we go back to page 1 of the English translation, but you can see on the B/C/S version, it was published in the Tanjug publication, but the source of this document needs to be redacted because it's a Rule 70 source. But you can see clearly from the document here that it was publicly -- that it was publicised and the date, the 28th of March, in Tanjug.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is Tanjug? Tanjug is a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you ...

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanjug was the official news service of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if it was published like that, why must it be a Rule 70 document? Who reads the Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that's a question for me, Your Honour, the answer lies in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I think the question for you was: Who reads Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who reads Tanjug. Okay, well, Tanjug is a news service, and they distribute their product the way other news services do, AP, for instance, to various media outlets both inside and outside the former Yugoslavia, and the material was published in many newspapers and broadcast over radio or television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then why does it become a Rule 70 document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, because we don't have that issue of Tanjug, and we have relied on -- and that we were provided this document by a Rule 70 source. So we are simply using the Rule 70 source document because we don't have the media article from 1991. And the Rule 70 provider requests that certain information be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's your understanding, Mr. Guy-Smith, that this is a Rule 70 document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's my understanding now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't know that before?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I'm going to have to check my records now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was whether you knew this --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. I just have to double-check that first. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you understand us to do in the meantime, hold on, wait for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, no, no, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on and admit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, carry on and admit. I understand what's going on. If I have any comments on it, they are certainly not fatal to the admission of this particular exhibit, and I will respond to your question once I have an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have Rule 65 ter number 06697 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, how did the Bosnian Serbs respond to this statement by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they maintained their position basically and issued another document on the 10th of June, 1991. When I say "they," again, I mean the SDS deputies in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In that document, did they set forth their position in relation to resolving the Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I could draw the Court's attention to page 6 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Page 6 and 7 of the English, Your Honour, and 6 and 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we are at page 6 in the English. I see it's 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the top of page 6 in the English, I would draw the Court's attention to the first paragraph, which I will read: "In republics which have more than one state-founding nation, citizens and nations may proceed to organise themselves into regions based on economic, cultural, information-related, ethnic and/or other interests. Regions (cantons, districts, provinces, et cetera) may have certain original powers in terms of legislation, justice and administration, and powers to regulate public utility services, like in some modern European countries." Then I would draw the Court's attention to the fourth and fifth paragraphs on that page: "Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a peculiar state shared by --" that really should read "of" - three equally sovereign nations and citizens can choose a uniform solution for its status in the," there's a word omitted, "joint state of Yugoslavia --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, are you giving the corrections as you pick them up from the Bosnian side also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've looked at the original on this, and the word "joint" is omitted there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, it is important because Mr. Guy-Smith has to know those kind of corrections, like we agreed the other day. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "... to choose a uniform solution for its status in the joint state of Yugoslavia if all three of its state-founding nations agree to it. If there is no such agreement, the uniform solution, regardless of its substance, cannot be foisted upon any one nation. Instead, a solution must be sought which does not threaten any of the nations, respecting their right to self-determination. In this respect --" In the next paragraph: "In this respect the Serbian people in BH are in a satisfactory position because they now share one state with other parts of the Serbian nation and can continue to exercise this historical and natural right. There is no way, apart from brute force, in which the Serbian people in BH can be separated from Yugoslavia and deprived of the protection of their interests in the federal state." So we see them restating the idea that they do not want to leave Yugoslavia and suggesting an internal reorganisation of BH of the formation of -- eventual possible formation of regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, there was reference in that document to regions. Can you briefly, and very briefly, describe for the Court what had happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to regionalization.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In April a community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina -- I'm sorry, of -- yes, of Bosnian Krajina was formed which brought together numerous municipalities in Western Bosnia that were under the control of the SDS and other communities of municipalities were also formed at that time in BH, in other regions. I'm not sure how many. The documentation is rather scanty. This is similar to the process that we saw in Croatia with the formation of communities of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. And this is April of what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in September, following, then, this position set forth by the Serbs that we have just looked at, the Bosnian Serbs, in this document, were there any other developments in relation to regionalization in September 1991?

Yes. In September a number of Serbian autonomous districts were formed, again similar to the process that we saw in Croatia, where communities of municipalities were transformed into Serbian Autonomous Districts. Again, the documentation is rather scanty on this, but, for instance, the communities of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina transformed itself into the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the statute for that region adopted on, I believe it was, the 15th of September, 1991, the new Autonomous Region of Krajina is described as an inseparable part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: By October, mid-October 1991, what was the situation in the Assembly, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

Well, by mid-October, that is, the 15th of October to be precise, the very thing that the Serbian Democratic Party leaders had feared happened, something that had been presaged by the statement by Alija Izetbegovic that we saw earlier; namely, the non-SDS deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted a resolution on the sovereignty and -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also basically disassociating itself from the federation, withdrawing its representatives from federal organs and proclaiming itself neutral in the -- as they put it, neutral between Croatia and Serbia. At this point the Court will remember that fighting was going on in Croatia. The SDS regarded this as a tremendous violation of the constitutional order and indeed breaking of certain promises that had been made to them by Alija Izetbegovic not to force such a resolution through the Assembly. They regarded those resolutions, as I say, a virtual declaration of independence, which they were strongly opposed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, how did they react, the Bosnian Serbs, the SDS?
Well, they had a lot of meetings, and they considered that the way forward, one result of the meetings was an announcement to the Serbian people, which they issued on the 16th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have Rule 65 ter number 06688, please. And that's page 1 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this the document to which you've just referred?

Yes. I'd direct the Court's attention to paragraph 1, which states: "At night of October 14th to 15th 1991, the deputy groups of SDA and HDZ, along with deputies of some opposition parties, applying political terror, attempted coup d'etat, by passing anti-constitutional decisions, with the objective to annul the tradition of joint life of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. By this act, the constitutional establishment has been endangered, which was based on sovereignty and equality of constitutive nations, while the gate has been opened to anarchy and chaos." That is their view of the situation. I would now call the Court's attention to paragraphs 4 and 5, perhaps even beginning with paragraph 3, which states: "The Serbian Democratic Party and its representatives at all levels of the government shall ensure the safety of Serbian people at all times, at any cost, using all means available." Paragraph 4 states: "If the constitutional order is not preserved," and there's a word missing here, it should read "in the Assembly of BH, Serbian people shall establish legal hierarchy in compliance with the constitution of SFRY, ensure," the proper translation here would be "respect of federal constitution, federal laws, civil and national rights, and shall organise its own legislative, executive and judicial system, which every sovereign nation is entitled to." Further: "By complying with the federal constitution and law consistently, we are supporting," again a word left out, "the work of federal organs, i.e., SFRY Presidency, Federal Assembly, and JNA, which is the only one available to prevent forceful breaking apart of Yugoslavia," the "which" referring to the JNA. Paragraph 5: "Sovereign nations shall decide on their destiny freely expressing their own will." "Serbian people shall remain in Federal state of Yugoslavia, unless otherwise decided at a plebiscite. Serbian people recognises the right to other constitutive and sovereign nations to conduct their plebiscites and decide on their future within Yugoslavia or out of it."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this document, this is -- we'd object at this time with regard to, first of all, the translation issues that arise because there are a number of them, and I believe it would be appropriate to have an official translation of this document. Second of all, there are some questions with regard, and I understand the procedure, the guidelines that we have, but there are some questions with regard to the authenticity of this document and what this document actually does represent. There is no date on this document -- I'm sorry, there is a date on this document. There's no stamp or signature on this document. There is an indication that it has some relationship to the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but beyond that, it's unclear. So there may be some issues with regard to its authenticity and whether or not the witness's assertion of who the document, in fact, can be attributed to is accurate. There are two different issues. One is the translation issue and the other is the issue with regard to authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess the translation, I thought we agreed the other day that it will go in under the strict understanding that it will be replaced with a subsequent translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine, fine. You see, my brain is not working as precisely as it should today, Your Honour. With regard to the second objection, then, I'll submit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Sutherland, with respect to the second objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would say it's a matter of weight that you give the document, if it doesn't have a stamp or a signature, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is the witness not in a position to explain the absence of those?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He may well be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you shed any light on the matter?

Well, as far as the providence of the document is concerned, I can state that it comes from the records of the Serbian Democratic Party which were seized by Bosnian authorities after the beginning of the war, if I can put it that way, in the spring of 1992. There was a large volume of documents that were seized from the headquarters of the SDS in Sarajevo, and this was among them. I also note that there is a fax line at the top of the page which indicates that this document was either faxed from or -- I think that's the origin fax line, faxed from the offices of the magazine Javnost in Sarajevo. Javnost was the official magazine of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But a faxed document cannot explain the absence of a signature, could it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. So that's the short answer: You have no explanation for that. There you are. We've been told the source of the document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understood the Chamber will give it whatever weight it deems appropriate at that time, and I'll remain -- I'll remain with the position we took. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may realise I hesitated a little bit. I was trying to remember the question I wanted to ask for clarification, Mr. Treanor. When you say it was seized from the SDS -- SDA -- SDS party offices by the Bosnian authorities, which Bosnian authorities -- Bosnian authorities of which ethnic group or of which institution? Because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. Well, I think colloquially we might refer to them as the Bosnian Muslim authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought colloquially you called them Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not use that term in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then we should clearly say Muslim, because they are Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Croats, and the -- the Bosnian Muslim authorities, those the ones you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, which were the -- remained in Sarajevo as the, I believe, internationally recognised government. I can also add, by the way, that it appears to be a sort of press release which I don't know it would require a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's a press release.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appears to be of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, okay, it is so admitted then, and may it be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P178, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, did the SDS establish a legal hierarchy?
Yes, they did, shortly after the declaration which we've seen. "Shortly after" meaning eight days later on the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Rule 65 ter number 06600 on the screen, please, and page 1 of the English and also the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 24th of October, the Club of Deputies of the SDS, which was the body that had issued the previous declarations we've seen, founded its own assembly. I would comment here that this shows the contrast between the political position of the SDS and the BH, as opposed to the political position between the SDS and Croatia. As result of the elections in Croatia in 1990, the SDS had only won two, three, or four seats in the Croatian Sabor, the Croatian Assembly, whereas the SDS, as I mentioned, had 72 representatives and was represented in the government. So their political base in Bosnia was much stronger. Their political importance within the general framework of that republic was much greater --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I do hate to interrupt. If Mr. Treanor could answer the question that was posed, as opposed to dealing with something else, that would be appreciated. I'm not trying to limit his answers whatsoever, but there was a question posed. On a number of occasions, the witness has a tendency to give us information which well be quite informative but it doesn't deal with the question posed. The question posed is very simply: Did the SDS establish a legal hierarchy?" That's at line 8 on page 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, the question was -- yes, fair enough. Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Treanor did answer that question and proceeded to tell you about the legal hierarchy that they did establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure you will remember that last week the Bench kept on admonishing Mr. Treanor to please be brief, concise, and to the point, and answer the questions as we don't have much time. Yes, for purpose of academics, it may very well be interesting to listen to you, Mr. Treanor, but we don't have that pleasure of that kind of -- that kind of pleasure, where we want answers to questions that are put only and nothing else. You may proceed. Therefore, I'm saying to you, Madam Sutherland, control your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if I could direct your attention to article V of that decision on the foundation of the Assembly of the Serbian People.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was their position in relation to any enactments passed in Bosnia by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina?
Well, I think paragraph V will have something to say about that. I have to point out that I do not have hard copies of the English translations at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That cannot be acceptable, Mr. Treanor. We agreed last week that you shall have the English version, you shall read from the English version, and correct them to the extent that you pick up mistakes. You can't be telling me that you don't have the English version before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was under the firm impression, Your Honour, that I was to be provided with the copies, and I was provided with copies on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we provided a binder to VWS to pass on to Mr Treanor at the beginning of his testimony today. I assumed that he had the binder in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, let's find out where that binder is, because then it means Mr. Treanor is -- again, is not reading from the same page as we are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can read the English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know you can. But if you don't have it before you, you can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's saying he can read it on the screen. On the e-court screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the screen. Why do you complain that you don't have the English version? It's right in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I had it prior to this, I could have compared it with the original. We can work off the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was not the problem. The problem was not a question of comparison. The problem was you just voluntarily told us that you're not reading from the English version; you don't have the English version. Now, if it is right in front of you, please avail yourself of it and read from it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think things may go quicker if we can locate the binder, and then Mr. Treanor can perhaps review the next several exhibits in the next break so he can have that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's part of the running of your case, ma'am. You'll do that. Carry on with the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph V we can say that it states: "The Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina shall recognise the validity of enactments passed by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina which are not contrary to the interests of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this also in relation to -- were the Assembly of the Serbian People prepared to recognise federal regulations at that time?
Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was that only if they were consistent with the federal regulations and didn't violate equal rights in the interests of the Serbian people?
They were prepared to recognise federal regulations, I think with that reservation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to Article VI of the document.

"The Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall recognise federal regulations and regulations of the republic, if they are consistent with federal regulations and if they do not violate the equal rights and interests of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be tendered into evidence -- submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's submitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P179, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the position, the SDS position, with respect to remaining in a joint Yugoslavia in -- at that time?
Well, they maintained their position, pushing to remain in Yugoslavia, and, in fact, this session of the Assembly passed a resolution to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Rule 65 ter number 06655 on the screen, please. Page 3 of the English translation and page 1 and 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was this the decision you just referred to, Mr. Treanor?
Yes, that's it. I would draw the Court's attention to paragraph 1, at the bottom of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is --
If that could be blown up perhaps a little more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: More importantly, if we can turn it over to the next page. We've seen the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Based on the right of self-determination, the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there doesn't seem to be a second page in this exhibit. Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the following exhibit, because this is the same page in the gazette as the previous decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It seems to be one of those technical days because we are not finding that the document that we presently have up on the screen in English comports with the document that we have as this particular 65 ter number, 6655 number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to help, Madam Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only have the ERN number for the document. I don't know if that's going to help the Registry or not. The ERN number that I want to be shown on the screen is SAO-1 -- sorry, ET-SAO1-0629 to 0630.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be, I think, page 3 of 3, then. We have that as a three-page document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the English translation, yes, so do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So do I, but we're trying to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just trying to help out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does Registry have the other two pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor -- Mr. Treanor, do you recall if that decision states that the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina will remain in the state of Yugoslavia together with Serbia, Montenegro, SAO Krajina, and the Serbian autonomous region of Slovenia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and others who expressed the same wish?
Yes, that's correct, but it requires that that decision be confirmed at a plebiscite of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, was your previous question answered by the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's not on the record, but Madam Registrar shook her head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, she did. I didn't see that. I thought you were jumping the gun before she's able to answer you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ERN number provided by the Prosecutor corresponds to the document on the screens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- which is a three-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I mark that document for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P180, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if I understand the state of this particular document, we are, for purposes of the record, we are presently relying on the witness's memory with regard to what the decision sets forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As I posed the question, Your Honour, yes. However, Mr. Treanor has the B/C/S available to him on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Treanor, can you confirm that that's your recollection through reviewing the document in B/C/S?
The next page would have to be shown on the screen. Yes, that's correct, II specifying that the decision will come into effect when it had been confirmed by a plebiscite of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the paragraph immediately above Roman numeral II is the text that was --
Yes, that comports with what you had suggested I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Rule 65 ter number 06755 could be placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what happened as a result of the plebiscite?

Well, a plebiscite was, in fact, held among the Serbian people in BH on the 9th and 10th of November, and that plebiscite produced an overwhelming majority in favour of the decision that we just saw. As a result of that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did they issue a decision in relation to that?
Yes. At the next session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in BH, the deputies passed a decision based on the results of that plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is this the decision that you were referring to that's on the screen now?
Yes. I would direct the Court's attention to paragraphs 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And basically was the territory that's mentioned in this decision the same as the last decision that we just mentioned?

Well, let me read that. It says: "Territories which are considered the territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia are territories of the municipalities, local communities and settlements in which on 9 and 10 November the plebiscite of Serbian and other peoples took place regarding their remaining in a joint Yugoslav state together with the Republic of Serbia, Republic of Montenegro, SAO, that is Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And when more than 50 per cent of registered voters of Serbian nationality, as well as citizens, members of other nations and nationalities, declared to remain in the joint state of Yugoslavia." Paragraph 2, which is a Roman II in the original, states: "Parts of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina from article 1 of this decision together with territories of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro, SAO Krajina, and SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, represent a core of a joint Yugoslav state." Paragraph 3, which is Roman III: "Municipalities, local communities, and inhabited places in which the plebiscite was not carried out may express their will to remain in the joint state as provided in Article 1 of this decision by means of a plebiscite or a decision of the assembly of their municipality, local community, or settlement, or they can organise in some other way."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, can I appeal to you to please control your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour. I undertake to do that. May that document be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't cut me short when I'm still talking, Madam Sutherland. I’m going to make you understand why I'm concerned. You ask a question, clearly asking the witness whether this was the territory was mentioned, and instead of mentioning it, he clearly says to you, Well, let me read it. And then he goes and reads out a whole paragraph that is going to be tendered into evidence that we can read later, taking a lot of time, and burdening the record unnecessarily, and you just let him go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take your point and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- it won't happen again. Could that exhibit be tendered -- be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why should we, if we have read it already? It's been read into the record. Why should we admit it? So that we can read it twice over? Read it in the record and then read it again as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the dates and the title of the document are actually in the record, Your Honour, and for those reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't ask any questions about dates and titles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, when was this decision issued?
This decision was issued on the 21st of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what's the actual full name of the decision?
The decision is entitled: "Decision Regarding Territories of Municipalities, Local Communities, and Inhabited Places in BH which are Considered the Territory of the Federal state of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the number of the decision, please.
This is decision number 36-02/91.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no need to admit this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, as we bring the document up, if you could give the Court your comment or opinion on the actual document without reading each of the paragraphs into the record, that would be helpful. We have a lot of documents to get through and not a lot of time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have Rule 65 ter number 06602 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just before we look at that document, Mr. Treanor, can you -- are you able to tell us what, if any, decisions were issued in relation to the Serbian autonomous regions? Very briefly. Very briefly.

The Assembly of the Serbian People also passed a decision verifying, that is, ratifying perhaps, the Serbian autonomous regions that had been formed, stating that they were to be part of BH as federal units in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When the Bosnian authorities sought recognition, what did the Bosnian Serbs do in relation to forming their own state?
They proceeded to establish further organs of power at this time and also to declare their intention to proceed to the formation of their own republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did they do this?
This would have been on the 21st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did they issue a decision in this regard?
They issued a decision to proceed to the formation of a republic, and they also appointed a council of ministers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did they do that in the document that you can see on the screen now?
No. At the bottom of the screen, the beginning of one document, it's there, and we should look at the next page as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's in the B/C/S?
Yes. At the bottom of the B/C/S page we see --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it has the number 21; is that correct?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is the second page of the English translation on the screen -- in e-court? Your Honour, I'm sorry, we don't seem to have the English translation of that document. May it be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification. May it please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P181, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Madam Sutherland, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take the break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may correct the record, I advised you previously that I had been advised that the binder was with VWS to give to Mr. Treanor before the commencement of testimony today; however, that's not the case. There was a miscommunication within the Office of the Prosecutor and the binder remained there. So I just wanted to correct the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can I just remind you before we start that we have a lot of documents to cover, and I would ask that you be as brief as possible in answering my questions.
Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The last document that we looked at was in relation to the decision to proceed to the formation of a Serbian republic. Did this, in fact, happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could have Rule 65 ter number 06604 on the screen, please, and page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the 9th of January, 1992, the Serbian Republic of BH was proclaimed by the Assembly of the Serbian People in BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the territorial delineation was going to be in relation to the new republic?
Briefly, it was to include the territories of the Serbian autonomous districts that had been formed in BH, as well as other territories which may wish to join.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What date was this declaration?
I think I mentioned the 9th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, you did, too. What did the declaration state in relation to the federal state of Yugoslavia? If I can direct your attention to Roman numeral II.
I'm sorry, this document is not in the binder I've been given. It stated, quite briefly, that the republic is part of the federal state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long after -- you mentioned yesterday the RSK had proclaimed the Republic of Serbian Krajina. What was the difference in time period between the RSK and the Bosnian Serbs in Serbia -- Bosnia?
I guess it would have been 19 days, from the 21st of December, 1991, to the 9th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, at that time was a commission set up called the Badinter Commission, and if so, what was their role in the events in Yugoslavia in early 1992, if you could briefly tell the Court.

The so-called Badinter Commission was established around this time in the closing months of 1991 by the European Community to rule -- I'm sorry, to offer recommendations, I think, as to how to proceed with international legal issues connected with the events in the former Yugoslavia, to examine the issue, for instance, the independence of individual republics and matters of that nature. I think I referred to it earlier when the RSK asked for recognition based on the guidelines that had been issued by the EC. And at this particular time in January, the Badinter Commission came out with some decisions, one of which basically said that the SRBiH had not yet filled the conditions for recognition and suggested that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, at this point I'm not clear as to whether or not the witness is now interpreting the legal decision or not, or whether he's giving his historical view of what an international legal commission proclaimed. I don't know whether or not this particular testimony is outside the expertise of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not my view that that's what the witness -- the witness isn't interpreting a legal issue. He's simply telling you what the Badinter Commission was set up for, what their role was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm specifically referring to page 37, lines 15 and 16, in which the witness states -- I'm sorry, it starts at 14: "And at this particular time in January, the Badinter Commission came out with some decisions, one of which basically said that the SRB BH had not yet filled the conditions for recognition and suggested that ..." at which point I rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an interpretation of legal conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was my concern at the time. For him to say that it basically says something, it may well require the interpretation of a legal opinion. Now, it's something that we can pursue perhaps when I stand to speak with the witness, but at this point in time, I viewed that in terms of the use of the term "basically" as an opinion with regard to how he interprets a legal decision. If we were having a discussion about, for example, let's say, the Tadic decision, and I suggested that it basically discussed or created a theory of liability that had yet to be dealt with in international law, I would be, as an attorney, interpreting a legal decision, and it's for that reason that I rise. If the Chamber is not in accordance, so be it. My concern was we were beginning to get into an area of him interpreting legal decisions. I don't believe he's being offered as an expert in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, my response to that is he's simply stating facts, and he's telling you what the Badinter Commission called for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you understand the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection says he doesn't say the Badinter Commission which stated A, B, C, D. He says "basically." He says the following, which suggests an interpretation of the report by the witness rather than telling us exactly what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, but the objection, as I understood it, was that he was interpreting a legal -- a legal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And by using the word "basically," he's giving us his interpretation of it. That's the nub of the objection. And he's not saying which literally says A, B, C, D, or which says A, B, C, D, but he says which "basically" says A, B, C, D. In other words, he's giving us a summary of what that says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Point taken, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if you can give the Court the objective facts, and then you can provide the Court with your opinion on those facts.

I didn't realise "basically" had a legal meaning. Not being a lawyer, I should have said "in brief," I suppose. I don't have the document in front of me, but it did refer at the end the possibility of holding a referendum in BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serbs issue any conclusions in relation to a common state for the Serbian people?
Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did they do this?
That would have been on the 26th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb republic adopt a constitution?
Yes. On the 28th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 06656 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, what should we do with 06644?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's so admitted. May it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just a clarification with the counsel, the document on the screen is 06604, as I heard counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke, Your Honour. It's 06604. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So 65 ter number 06604 will be Exhibit P182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can have Rule 65 ter number 06656 on the screen, please. Page 2 of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, is this the constitution that you were referring to that was adopted on the 28th of February, 1992?
Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what organs did it allow to be set up?
This constitution established as the principal organs of power in the republic an assembly, a government, a presidency, and of course courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I direct your attention to Article 3 of the constitution. What -- is reference made there to the fact that the republic is part of the federal state of Yugoslavia?
Yes. The article quite simply states that: "The republic is part of the federal state of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is admitted into evidence. Will be given an exhibit number. I'll say that again after I switch on my mic. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was any other legislation adopted at this time by the Bosnian Serb republic?

Yes. At this same session the Assembly adopted several pieces of legislation relating to the functioning of the new republic. It adopted a constitutional law which contained transitional provisions until the provisions of the constitution could be carried out, for instance, who would act as the Assembly until the elections for the Assembly were held. It also adopted other laws, such as the law on government, the law on ministries, a law on internal affairs, and a law on national defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who was to carry out the functions, or what provisions were made -- sorry. What provisions were made in relation to a president, for example?

Well, under the terms of the constitutional law, the powers of the president were to be exercised by the two Serbian members of the Presidency of the SRBiH until such time as a president was elected under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were those two members?
Those two members were Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was the -- you mentioned the law on defence and the law on internal affairs. When were they to become operational? When was the law to be enacted?

Well, they were to become operational eight days after their publication in the Official Gazette of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but then an event which took place on the 23rd of March, 1991, so they would have become operational on the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that the constitution was proclaimed on the 27th of February, 1992, and that the -- as a result of the constitution, the Serbian republic would remain as part of Yugoslavia. What, in fact, were the prospects of them remaining within Yugoslavia at this time?
I believe the date of the constitution was the 28th of February. The prospects for them actually remaining in Yugoslavia at this time were not very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Rule 65 ter number 06668 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason for that was that, although it appeared to be a simple matter to remain within the SFRY, in fact the -- all the republics of the SFRY had -- or many of the republics had been recognised as independent by that time, and Serbia and Montenegro were in the process of forming, if I can call it that, a new state consisting of Serbia and Montenegro. And the idea of the Bosnian -- the Bosnian Serb areas or the Croatian Serb areas remaining or being part of that state would have caused tremendous international complications for the new state in the view of the Belgrade leaders; therefore, they wished to proceed with the formation of that state, including only the republics of Serbia and Montenegro and not any portions of neighbouring states -- or of -- at that time Croatia was recognised as a state and Bosnia, which was in the course of becoming recognised as a state.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the beginning of March, was this discussed within the Presidency of the SFRY?

Yes. There was a meeting at the Presidency of the SFRY at the beginning of March, on the 2nd of March to be precise. It was attended by members of the Presidency and other officials of the SFRY, including the acting secretary of national defence, General Blagoje Adzic, and numerous Croatian and Bosnian Serb leaders including Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Goran Hadzic, and Milan Martic, for instance. They discussed issues relating to the future of the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia, in view of the fact that they would not be able to be part of the new state that was being formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that we go to page 35 of the English translation and page 20 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what did Radovan Karadzic have to say at that meeting in relation to the Republic of Bosnia -- the Bosnian Serb republic joining Yugoslavia or joining Serbia?

Well, he spoke in favour of a reconsideration of that decision by the Belgrade leaders, especially in view of the fact that the plebiscite of the Serbian people had been carried out and the republic had -- the Serbian Republic of BH had passed a constitution saying it was part of Yugoslavia. It was made clear that that decision would stand, and he recognised the reasons for that decision and accepted it. In this passage we can see him saying: "We decided not to demand joining Serbia. We also do not demand staying in Yugoslavia at all costs. We can see what we have been criticised for, and we can see what has created troubles for Serbia and Montenegro."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did Mr. Adzic say about the matter, or General Adzic?

General Adzic didn't express a direct view on the political issue but did explain to the Croatian and Bosnian Serbs the military arrangements that were being made for the Serbian areas in those republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 50 of the English translation - I'm not sure what page it is in e-court - and page 38 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did Mr. Adzic say there would be -- what, if anything, did he say in relation to options available in relation to the JNA?
Well, he said on page 51 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm a bit -- and I do apologise for interrupting. I'm a bit confused because the document that I see on the screen in English does not refer to Mr. Adzic in English, and I don't know what it's doing in the original. I think there's a -- there's some kind of synchronicity problem at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was my concern as well. I said I wanted page 50 because the proper pages weren't coming up in e-court. I'm informed that it's the second translation attachment to the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second translation attachment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The second translation document that's attached to the e-court system, Your Honour. It's all foreign to me, I'm sorry. I'm simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you want to call that document on to the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 97. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that second document, the attachment goes to page --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's actually page 50 of the translation of the document, but it appears on page 97 of e-court of the second translated document that's attached to that Rule 65 ter number within e-court, I'm advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you please go back one page to page 96. If you could blow up around the middle of the page, please, where it's Adzic -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, my question, Mr. Treanor, was: Did Adzic talk about different options for the JNA?
Yes, he did, but I think that's at a later point in his presentations in this meeting. It's not on this page. On this page he refers to the stationing of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can now go to the following page, down the bottom of page 97 and the top of page 98, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that the passage that you just referred to, that you were talking about? Down the bottom, it starts with the word "Therefore ..." It's the very last word on that page. The paragraph starts: "I believe that a decision will have to be made ..."
Oh, yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the word "Therefore," and then if we go to the next page.
Yes. "Therefore, there can be two things. Either the army will stay there ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have the next page on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "There" being BH. "... until a political situation is found or we will go to war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia. If we have no other choice, we will go to a civil war. Then let it be Lebanon. We have no other choice because the others will make us do so."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, you have indicated that this document seems to have very many pages. Are you tendering the pages that you've referred to, or are you tendering the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would seek to tender the whole document, Your Honour, because it will be referred to with other witnesses in the trial, during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I refer you to our guidelines, ma'am. I guess you've got a copy of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do we say about tendering voluminous documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It says that relevant -- this is paragraph 24, Your Honour, of your ruling. Sir, we can seek to have the portions that Mr. Treanor has referred to into evidence. I am at this stage unable to give you the e-court numbers, so perhaps if we can mark that document for identification until I can come back to you with the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what is wrong with admitting the pages that we have referred to, and if other witnesses want to use some other pages, we can admit their pages in, rather than put in a minimum of 97 pages, it looks like two-thirds of which we might not read.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. That's what I just said. But I said that I couldn't give you the page numbers at the moment because the first cite I took you to, page 35, did not come back -- page 35 of the translation didn't appear on the screen, and so I want to give you the exact e-court page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I hadn't understood where you were going.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if we could mark ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, remember, you referred us to two translations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the second translation you called it as an attachment in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I wonder if you can clarify which of each of those documents you want admitted, which pages of each of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, and at this stage, I'm not able to tell you that because I have certain numbers written down on my index which aren't correlating to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To the e-court pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- to the e-court pages. So I would ask we mark that exhibit for identification, and then I can come back to you with the actual page numbers of that big document that I would like to have tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll do so. Then the document -- Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
