utterances.text: Excuse me, if I'm might. I am being told by people who read a language that I don't -- that these two pages are -- don't comport with each other, that they're not synced up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sutherland --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wanted to say "Mr. Treanor." I'm so sorry to you and to you, too, ma'am. May I ask you to fall back to the extra job that I asked you to exercise for us, that is, to check whether the translation we have on the screen does comport with the original we have on the screen. What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it doesn't appear to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the two pages don't appear to contain the same passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do you think the one is a translation of the other, or do you feel it's not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They appear to be different pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist, it looks --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think if I understand it, at least from the information I'm getting, that whatever the page is in the original and whatever it says, we do not have in the English. The English page that is presently -- that was presently up is not the same as the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't tell us what is on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist, I think that the page that was on the B/C/S page was the very start of Adzic's speaking, and so the B/C/S would need to go over one or two pages in order to catch -- to be the equivalent text of what was shown in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's why -- I guess that's why Mr. Guy-Smith stood up. Then make sure that we've got corresponding pages before we decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That passage would be on page 41 of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see we're at page 42 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the B/C/S can be taken back one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's it. Are we now -- are the two languages on the same page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two -- that passage, the translation of each page does not correspond in the two languages. They overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, because I was going to say I don't see the name "Carrington" in the B/C/S, which is slap-bang in the middle of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I took Mr. Treanor to two passages at the beginning of Adzic's speech, which was on that other page, and then the one that was on page 51 and 52 of the English transcript, so those are the two portions that I would seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought we had another point we were tendering, and I was trying to make sense what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm trying to -- we can see now that Carrington's name is coming up in the middle of the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But what I would like someone to do, Mr. Treanor or the Registry or case manager, to inform us as to what page in the B/C/S and in the English the two passages that I referred Mr. Treanor to, and that's starting -- Adzic's speech: "I think that we should not mention the Yugoslav People's Army in today's announcement." That's the first quote I took him to. And then the second one, starting on page 51 of the English translation, I don't know where in the B/C/S: "Therefore, there can be two things. Either the army will stay there until a political situation is found or we will go to war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia." Those are the two passages and a few more lines down that I took Mr. Treanor to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, are you able to find the two pages on which those two quotations appear?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could try and locate the e-court pages, which I will come back to you in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, fine. When you have located them, can you upload -- what do you say in your language, you upload or -- okay. They are admitted into evidence, then, and can they be given an exhibit number for now. You wanted this exhibit to be MFIed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because I was unable to give you the correct pages, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Then give it an exhibit number, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So that will be Exhibit P184, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, Mr. Adzic mentioned that the army would stay there, i.e., in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As they were to stay there, was the JNA giving any direct assistance to the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Rule 65 ter number 06800 on the screen. Your Honour, this was a document that Mr. Harmon used in his opening statement and the Prosecution was to provide the Trial Chamber with an English translation of the legend to the document. However, I've been advised that the legend is not connected in e-court under this exhibit number. It's, in fact, another number which I will call up in a moment. But you will see the English translation, then, of the document that was referred to, and we will get to the legend in one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the quantity of weapons that -- so we're talking -- we're talking March 1992. What was the quantity of weapons that the JNA provided to the Serbs in Bosnia?
The answer to that question is provided on page 6 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 6 of the translation and page - I'll try my luck - 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the number of weapons?
In the middle of the English translation page, we can see under point (f) the statement that the JNA has distributed 51.900 weapons, 75 per cent; in the SDS, 17.298.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you tell the Court who this document is from, his position, and the date of the document.
That document is a report by General Kukanjac, who was the commander of the 2nd Military District of the JNA headquartered in Sarajevo, and the date is the 20th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can take you to paragraph 5, "Volunteer Forces in the 2nd Military District," does it give a definition in this document as to who volunteers are?
Well, it says who they aren't. This is a discussion of volunteer forces attached to the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who are they not?

Under point (c), under 5, it states that: "No volunteers are potential conscripts for regular units," or war units, "of the 2nd Military District and only a small number are from the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, the volunteer units are not part of the JNA and the TO establishment structure."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, my own clarification. We're saying there are only a small number from the TO of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then in the same breath, at the end we say that they are not part of the TO establishment structure. Can we give the name of that last TO? Which TO is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina, saying that they're not part of the TO, only a small number are from the TO. So these are volunteer forces in addition to the TO and the JNA in BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, just for my clarity, can you just give me a very single-worded answer? Of which army is the TO at the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- the TO in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Or is that a more general question, what is the TO a part of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, of which army. I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- this TO of which these volunteers are not a part of, so the TO of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TO is part of the Armed Forces of the SFRY. It is not part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. Maybe I should have said, "of which country?" So this last TO refers to the TO of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, which is organised on a republic level, so in this case we're talking about BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you confused me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, you can't say it's of the SFRY and then say of the BH in the same breath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH was still part of the SFRY at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, the TO of the BH cannot be -- the TO of the BH is TO of the SFRY, and therefore these two TOs that you're referring to are the same TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you can say they are part of this but not part of this. It doesn't make sense, that statement, then, because it is saying they are -- they compose a small number from the TO of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which you say at that time was part of the SFRY; therefore, it is a misnomer to call them the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are actually the TO of the SFRY. But in the same breath you're saying, "In other words, the volunteer units --" I'm not saying you say, but the statement says: "In other words, the volunteer units are not part of the JNA and the TO establishment structure." Now, at that time there is only one TO establishment structure of the SFRY. They are part of it, constituting a small number, but they are not part of it. Can you explain that discrepancy -- apparent discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TO is part of the -- is a very large organisation that covered the whole of the SFRY, and it was considered to be part of the Armed Forces of the SFRY. The establishment structure of the TO is based on the republics, so that is the first level of command below the Presidency of the SFRY, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each republic had its own TO that, under certain circumstances, in a war, came under the command of the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH was still part of the SFRY --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and had its own TO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. But then that TO in the BH is part of the TO establishment of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But now to say some people, small number, who are members of the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina but not members of the TO establishment structure is a contradiction logically, if I follow what you are explaining logically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in discussing the volunteer units, saying that only a small number of the volunteers are from the TO, so they're not in the TO. Why some of them should be from the TO at all, I do not know. But I understand this document to say that most of the volunteers are not part of the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation} I'm not sure I understand. Maybe I will say this in French. It seems to me that what this paragraph states is that the volunteers come originally from the TO, the Territorial Defence, but are not part of the Territorial Defence; is that right? But originally they come from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it says only a small number are from the TO, so some of them were from the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking about a small number only. And if I understand what Judge Picard is saying, would this mean that they have resigned from the TO to make themselves volunteers, and that's why they are not part of -- they are no longer part of the TO establishment structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, I do not know why they should be part -- how that took place. I do not know how that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can't take the matter any further. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we can have Rule 65 ter number for the attachment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's dispose of 06800, please, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would seek to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the index or the legend that's attached to that document is part of Rule 65 ter number 05698, if that could be brought onto the screen. Your Honour, that was the English -- you can see the English translation, and that's the document that was requested during the opening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, that's -- do you agree that that is the legend that's attached to the Kukanjac document, that's referred to in the Kukanjac document?
Sorry, which legend?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document that's on the screen at the moment, do you agree that that's the legend that's referred to in the Kukanjac document?
I'm not sure which legend is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to paragraph 5, volunteer units in the second military district zone are indicated on the map and in the legend in great detail, and then it lists the number of weapons that are provided, and that is 69.198, and then in paragraph (f) you gave a breakdown of those weapons distributed by the JNA and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I'm asking you, you've reviewed these documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is that this document that you've referred to as a legend does not give us information about weapons but about men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That lists the number of men per municipality of volunteers, and it says that the JNA has distributed -- I'm sorry, if I can take Mr. Treanor to it, rather than myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Paragraph (f) of this document, Mr. Treanor, gives the breakdown of the weapons distributed. And you mentioned that the JNA had distributed 51.900 weapons, which was 75 per cent, and the SDS had distributed 17.298. If you add those two figures together, do you get the total amount -- the total number of volunteers --
Yes, which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- volunteer forces, which is referred to in paragraph 5?
69.198, yes, which is a number that also appears in subparagraph (b), under 5 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so --
-- the enlisted men number, 69.198.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so this legend that's attached to this document lists the municipality and the number of men, with a grand total of 69.198, which corresponds to the number of weapons that have been distributed in paragraph (f).
Yes, the two numbers correspond, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Am I right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so admitted. May it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, after this date, i.e., the 27th of May, 1992, did the negotiations still continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could have Rule 65 ter number 06612 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, negotiations were continuing after the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware of National Security Council?
There was a Bosnian Serb National Security Council, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was that set up?
On the 27th of March, 1992, by the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I misspoke a moment ago when I said that after this date and the document being the 20th, I said the 27th. But the National Security Council was set up on the 27th of March. What occurred in Bosnia at the beginning of April 1992.
Well, a lot happened in Bosnia at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In particular in relation to --
A very important development was the international recognition of the independence of BH on the 6th and 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is that --
This would have been the recognition by the EC states and the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did it take place on the 1st of April or on the 6th and 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 6th and 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the question was -- where is the question now? I thought the question was: What happened on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, beginning of April, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The beginning of April. I'm so sorry, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the EC members issue a written declaration?
Yes. Written statements were issued on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is this the document that we see on the screen before you?
No, this is not the EC declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. What is this document that's in front of us in relation to the declaration on recognition?
This is a media report about a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the media in question being Belgrade Radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And does it state what the EC and member states decided in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Direct us to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I really apologise. We'll leave that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What impact did the declaration that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you're withdrawing the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What impact did the declaration of independence of Bosnia have on the development of the Republic of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina?
The international recognition of the independence of BH prompted the Bosnian Serb Assembly to declare the independence of the Serbian Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did that occur?

That occurred at a session that took place in -- on the night of the 6th of April and continued into the early morning, I believe, of the 7th of April, 1992. That was indicated in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serbs -- did the Bosnian Serb Assembly conduct an Assembly session on the 12th of May, 1992?
Yes, there was a session on that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have Rule 65 ter number 06277, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the main aim of this session and its importance to the Bosnian Serbs?
The importance of this session was that it dealt with certain matters of the restructuring of the Bosnian Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What session number was it?
This is the 16th session. It was the first session after the session that proclaimed independence early in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So what were the certain matters on restructuring that occurred at this session?
Well, the two principal matters were a restructuring of the organ of the Presidency and the formation of an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Assembly adopt any goals in relation to the Serbian people?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 67 of the English translation. It's on page -- I'm sorry, it's on page 13, not page 67. It's on page 13 of the English translation, and it's on page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court what were those goals that were announced at the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

Well, I can do that by reading, perhaps, the -- just the first paragraph that has been marked on the copy I've been given, which is the first full paragraph in the middle of the page, "The Serbian side ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just paraphrase it, sir. If it's going to be tendered, then I don't think you need to read all of that long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This paragraph states that -- it states that the goals which Radovan Karadzic is speaking about in this speech were --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the first goal? What was the first goal that was announced?
He says that the first goal is separation from the other two national communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Meaning? Who's he referring to there?
The Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the -- how many goals were there? How many goals were announced?
There were six goals altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that's the first one. What was the second one?
The second goal - this is going to the next paragraph on that page - the next strategic goal, it seems to me he says, is a corridor between Semberija and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the importance of that corridor?

The area being referred to is along the southern bank of the river Sava, which was the northern boundary of Bosnia, and that was the only land route that connected the eastern part of the Bosnian Serb republic with the western part of the republic, and it was therefore important as the land route which connected Serbia with many portions of the RSK in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the third goal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my finger doesn't work. Does it connect Serbia, or does it connect the east and the western parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour. The eastern part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina bordered on Serbia, therefore linking the eastern part of the Serbian republic with the western part, also linked Serbia as well as the eastern part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the larger part of the Serbian Republic of Krajina, that is, the Serbian republic in Croatia, because it does not have any land border with Serbia or the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And does Dr. Karadzic state in relation to the second goal that it is of greatest interest "because we cannot have unity of Serbian states if we do not have that corridor"?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the third strategic goal that was announced?

The third goal was in the next paragraph, the following paragraph. He states: "The third strategic goal is to establish a corridor in the Drina Valley, that is, elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is he referring to there? What are the two worlds?

Well, I'm not precisely sure what two worlds he's referring to. The Drina, for much of its course, was the border between Serbia and BH, in this case portions of the Serbian Republic of BH. A corridor in the Drina Valley would have linked the north-eastern part of the Serbian Republic of BH with its south-eastern part in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, if we could have as the page in Serbian, and I'll use the ERN number because that's the way that it's being referred to me, it's 0214-9447, that would have the two -- that would be the Serbian original page, and I was just informed that that puts the two of them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It also would have made portions of the border along the Drina accessible, the corridor would have made it accessible to the Bosnian Serb republic and given them communication in those particular areas with Serbia. That entire area, that is, the Drina Valley, was not under the control of the Serbian Republic of BH at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the fourth goal?
The fourth strategic goal is discussed in the following paragraph. I'll just read the first sentence again: "The fourth strategic goal is establishment of the border on the Una and Neretva rivers."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What's the importance of this goal?

This goal specifies two other portions of the external border of the Serbian Republic of BH; namely, the Una river, which is in the north-western part of BH. Part of BH is on the western bank of the Una, which would be the left bank. At this point -- in this goal, he appears to be claiming only the right bank, the eastern bank. The Una ran north through BH into the Sava river, which, as I mentioned earlier, forms the northern border of BH, or in this case, if the corridor were formed, in large part, the northern border of the Serbian Republic of BH. The Neretva is in the south. It flows through Mostar down to the sea. The establishment of a border on the Neretva, and I think the reference is again to the eastern bank of the Neretva which, in this case, it runs in the opposite direction, would be the left bank, as being claimed, would have given the Bosnian Serb republic control of the whole of the eastern Herzegovina. A large part of that territory was not under its control at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the fifth strategic goal that was announced?

The fifth goal was dealt with in the following paragraph, which states: "The fifth strategic goal is division of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts and implementation of an effective state government in each of these two constituent states."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go over to the next page on the English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was stated by Karadzic as being the importance of that goal?

Well, he states further in that paragraph that: "The battle in and for Sarajevo is seen strategically and tactically as a decisive importance because it does not allow the establishment of even the illusion of a state. Alija does not have a state while we have part of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't know whether or not the witness is reading now in English or from Serbian, because what I'm reading is different. I have it -- "because it does not allow even for the illusion," and the existence of the word "establishment" is not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm reading what is in front of me in hard copy, "because it does not allow --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I withdraw what I just said. I've got two screens going right now, and I've made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apparently we have -- apparently what seems to be the case is that we have three separate translations for the same document that have been supplied to us, so that's why that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the final CLSS translation that we're looking at at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what was the sixth and final goal that was announced on the 12th of May?
The sixth goal is dealt with in the following paragraph, and I'll just read the first sentence: "The sixth strategic goal is the access of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the sea."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what's the importance of that goal?

Well, I think many states consider having access to the sea important, and the only access that BH had to the sea is a very small portion of the Dalmatian coast, and it was not under the control of the Serbian Republic of BH at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, those goals were announced by -- strategic goals were announced by Dr. Karadzic. Did anyone else from the Bosnian Serb leadership give their opinion as to which of the goals were the most important?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who was that?
Well, I think several people probably addressed various goals, but Momcilo Krajisnik certainly indicated what he thought was the most important goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 49 of the English translation and page -- it's on page 37 of the B/C/S. I don't know what page number in e-court, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you're looking for the page number in e-court, what do you think of the convenience? Maybe that will give you more time to find the page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's possible, if we could just deal with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what does Mr. Krajisnik say is the most important goal or goals?
I would direct the Court's attention to the bottom of the page, the bottom of this page, just before the first underlined portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK SAYS
utterances.text: "As for the goals, I would just like to offer an explanation, since I have also taken part in adopting these goals. We must make a choice regarding one thing. The first goal is the most important in relation to all other goals. All other goals are subitems of the first."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at a quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Madam Sutherland, I'm advised that the pages that you are going to search for have been identified. Can we just give it -- the admission regularised.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the pages that are tendered from P184, which is currently marked for identification are the following: The English e-court pages are page 1, page 96, page 97, page 98, and page 81, out of a total of 145 pages. And the B/C/S pages in e-court are page 1, page 20, page 38, page 41, page 84, and page 86 out of a total of 155 pages, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could Rule 65 ter number 09235 be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Madam Sutherland, I think you have -- before you do that, could we finalise 65 ter 06277, Madam Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't finished with that document as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you're calling another one?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I want to intersperse this one. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what will be coming up on the screen is a map, and I would like you to take the Court very quickly through strategic goals numbers 2 to 5 -- 2 to 6 in order for them to have a better understanding of the evidence that you just gave before the break in relation to the strategic goals, if you can. So, with respect to strategic goal number 2, the corridor between Semberija and Krajina, can you explain briefly to the Judges, in relation to the map, that strategic goal.

Yes. Immediately above the word "corridor" the Court can see the red line, which is the northern boundary of BH, and it follows the course of the river Sava and, for part of its distance, the river Una, and the corridor would have been along the southern bank of the river connecting the two parts. They are labeled Semberija and Bosnia and Krajina. Part of what is in the middle of BH was not under the control of the Serbian Republic of BH at this time, so they only controlled a very thin strip along the course of that border, the river in the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The third strategic goal refers to the establishment of a corridor in the Drina Valley. Can you take the Court to --
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- that goal?

The eastern border of BH is indicated by a red line again, and the blue line is the course of the river Drina. As the Court can see, it follows the border for much of its distance and departs from the border at a certain point and continues further south. Actually, okay, it comes from the south. And again, the whole distance of this river was not under the control of the Serbian Republic of BH at this time, and gaining such control would have enabled -- facilitated a connection between Semberija in the north and the southern portion of the republic, the south-eastern portion, which is around the word "Neretva" down there, which is Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so to the left -- left bank of the Drina is Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the right bank of the Drina is what?
Is Serbia, along the portion of the river that is also marked red.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The fourth strategic goal is to establish a border on the Una river and the Neretva river. Can you explain to the Court using the map that goal?

Yes. The course of the Neretva river is marked in blue, looping around the word "Neretva" and, as the Court can see, it flows into the sea in Croatia. Moving the border to that line, at least the western part of the loop, would have given the Serbian Republic of BH control of the whole of Eastern Herzegovina, and if they took the whole course -- the whole eastern bank, it would have, of course, given them access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The fifth strategic goal is the division of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts. I think that's obvious where Sarajevo --
Sarajevo is in the middle of the map. In relation to access to the sea, other -- there were other possibilities for gaining access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is the sixth strategic goal, access to the sea?

Without taking the eastern bank of the Drina within Croatia, if they were able to gain control of the part of BH which -- of BH which goes to the sea, which is indicated by the little loop just below the words "Access to the sea," that was BH's access to the sea, the small port there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May the map be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Returning now to Rule 65 ter number 06277, the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, Mr. Treanor, did -- who was appointed as -- you said that the 16th session passed laws in relation to the forming of the army, of the Bosnian Serb army. Who was appointed commander of that army?
The military commander that was appointed on this occasion was General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, at this session did he talk -- did he make reference to any of the goals?
He made some references which appear to relate to the goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could turn to e-court number 35 of the English translation and page 28 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did Mr. -- General Mladic say at that session in relation to the goals, as you -- as you understand it?
Well, right in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- as framed and as the question has been asked thus far, it calls for a level of speculation as to what is in the mind of the author, if we're in a situation where we're talking about directly somebody saying something, so there's not this interpretive aspect of what somebody is saying. That's a different matter. So if I could perhaps know where we're focused here with regard to this relatively lengthy conversation, I'll know whether or not my concern is that of speculation or not, which is he said, He appears to, which is distinct from with regard the goals he stated that, or he responded in a fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, my next question -- Mr. Treanor's answer was he made some references which appear to relate to the goals, and my next question was: "What did he say in relation to the goals as you understand it," meaning that you say that he appeared to make some expression in relation to the goals. That's what I was wanting Mr. Treanor to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, he's now being asked to perform a function of a fact-finder. I think this is a matter which the question is asked, especially in light of the answer given, and this is outside of -- outside of the purview of his expertise, and it also calls for speculation. If the document here is one of those situations where it speaks for itself, the Chamber can read it as easily as anyone else and can make a determination of what they believe its import to be, whatever that import may be. His interpretation does not assist in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand what the objection is all about. You rose up, Mr. Guy-Smith, after the question, "What did General Mladic say at that session in relation to the goals, as you understand it?" There's no "appears to relate" in that sentence. The "appears to relate" is in former sentence which you didn't object in the previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I should have jumped up quicker, Your Honour. If you take the two in conjunction, and "as you understand it," what he understands it to be is, apart from being vague and speculative, is irrelevant, what he understands it to be. Mr. -- General Mladic made a statement, whatever that statement may be. That statement is apparently open to interpretation. Now, this witness is not offered as a psychologist for purposes of what's in General Mladic's head. He's not offered for purposes of rendering opinion as to what the internal thinkings of General Mladic. He's offered to speak about objective facts and objective events that account for information of a historical and political nature which allows you to make a determination of their import. But what he understands this to mean, among other things, apart from being speculative, outside the purview of his expertise, is irrelevant. I could tell you what I understand it to mean, and if I were to testify about what I understood it to mean, I think you would rightfully say, Well, thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith, but what your understanding is is not particularly relevant. You can make an argument as to what the perception you have of a fact, but that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say? If you don't, I am ready to rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't agree, but you can make a ruling, or I can approach you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't have anything to say, then the objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, did Mr. Mladic -- General Mladic say in that session -- did he advise the session whether he had met with the leadership in Belgrade at that meeting? Was anything -- was anything discussed in relation to that?
Yes, he made reference to a meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did he say in relation to that? If I can --

In the middle of the page we're looking at -- I realise it's very hard with this passage to say exactly where it is. But in the line beginning with "Many of you ..." "Many of you have helped me. I already said this a few days ago. I kept on repeating certain things. I said this in Nevesinje before the top leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and before an even more select political leadership in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can take you to the sentence beginning "Please ..." which is just before that sentence.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does he mention anywhere about -- about goals being set for themselves?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does he say?
He says: "Please, let us not set before ourselves goals that will bring us down. Let us set before ourselves the goals we can achieve."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say the sentence that you just quoted a moment ago.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That many people have helped him and that he discussed certain things --
Yes, that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he kept on repeating certain things, and he said this: "In Nevesinje before the top leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and before an even more select political leadership in Belgrade."
That's the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he also make reference in that session in relation to keeping the work of what they were doing secret?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he say in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 38 of the English and page 28, I think, of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does General Mladic say about the work that they're doing?
Well, just above the middle of the page in English, in the line beginning with the words "About when to keep mum ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it may be on page 29 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the sentence and blow it up, starting "And please, ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's in a couple lines above, beginning with: "Whatever else there is, to keep it short, and please, let us not only put our minds into what we are doing, but let us also think thoroughly about it and let us be cautious about when to keep mum. No, the thing that we are doing needs to be guarded as our deepest secret."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When -- do you know when these strategic goals were actually published?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I normally have not risen for this reason, but this is a level of cherry-picking that I think potentially offends. If read, the language before and after, that particular statement, I think, puts it into that proper context, and I think it would be appropriate at this time rather than a later point in time for me to say, Well, you read sentence number 3 and 4, you should read sentence number 1 and 2 and 5 and 6. If this particular passage, or these particular two sentences are read in the context of its entirety, then the Chamber is in a position to take a -- an intelligent and objective analysis of what's being discussed there, if that can even be done. But certainly just picking out those two particular sentences and then tying them in to whatever the Prosecution theory is is not appropriate and certainly does not achieve what we're supposed to be doing here, which is to see that the truth emerges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've simply taken Mr. Treanor to two passages, one about the goals and one about the fact that he wants to keep the work that they're doing secret. I have simply asked Mr. Treanor, does he know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We know what you have done, madam. What is your response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm saying it's unfounded. I'm directing Mr. Treanor to a completely different question. I'm asking him when the goals were published. I have moved away from --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I am objecting -- I am objecting to your moving away because you are, in my respectful submission, mischaracterising what is being said there, and the Prosecution is engaged in cherry-picking with regard to the statement made by General Mladic. I mean, if I go up a sentence before, then the passage would read as follows: "I believe that at this very moment it is very important to place at the head of the Serbian people both --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want to read the whole thing, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want you to read anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very sorry. You are going to have an opportunity to cross-examine, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am, and for the most part I've left it alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Guy-Smith, are you now wanting the Prosecution to direct its examination according to how you want it? If you are going to cross-examine, obviously when you do do that, you will come to this page and quote everything that you need to have quoted to put what was said in the examination-in-chief in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. And for the most part this is something I have left alone. I find this one to be, in my estimation, of particular moment because, as we know, although this is an adversarial process under two specific notions; one is the doctrine of completeness, and the second is the duty of the prosecutor is not merely to convict but also to see that justice is done. When cherry-picking that presentation of the evidence, in my respectful submission, offends not one but both of those particular principles, which does not mean that these are not matters I will raise in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, then, how does the Chamber get the Prosecutor to ask questions she doesn't want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe -- well, part of it is perhaps through the either gentle or forceful objection of the Defence, and the other is within the context of the recognition of what the precise duties are. I think I understand. The Chamber's position is that it is preferable, based on what you've said thus far, that when I have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness, I can point out those particular points. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this whole page is going to be tendered. There's no way the Prosecution can tender only those lines without tendering the entire page which forms the context that you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if that's -- if that's the case, then I have some comfort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you ever think it wouldn't be the case that the page would be tendered together with those sentences?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was -- I have been concerned that in terms of redaction and cutting that we may be in that position, yes, having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it is practically impossible, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I've actually been in a situation where I've seen that occur so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where they cut and paste from the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where they cut or redacted and cut from the page and then presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When that happens and you believe that the context of the -- of what is being cut is being lost, stand up and object. At this point, the objection is overruled. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, the question that I put to you was: Do you know when these goals were published?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when was that?

In November 1993, the Official Gazette published a document which, I believe, was entitled the resolution or decision, conclusion, probably of the Assembly, which contained a very abbreviated version of the strategic goals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Treanor. You've answered the question in the first three lines -- three words. Can you ask the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can document number 06732 be put on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what was specifically was the impact on the command structure? You said that they had formed their own army, but who was to be in command of the army?
Well, the overall commander of the new army was the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as of that stage, I think, as of the 12th of May, what was the situation in relation to the president of the Serbian republic?

Well, the president had not been elected. The two acting presidents had been exercising the powers of the president of the republic, and on the 12th of May the Assembly passed an amendment to the constitutional law that restructuring the provisional/transitional Presidency, if you will, by forming a three-member Presidency which would exercise the powers of the presidents of the republic until such time as the president was chosen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were the members of the three-member presidency?
The three members were Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, who had been the acting presidents, and Radovan Karadzic was elected as the third member.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention to amendment III of the document in front of you. First of all, can you tell the Chamber what this decision is in relation to the constitution, or how it relates to the constitution, I should better say?

The decision that's mentioned on the previous page is the decision proclaiming the amendments to the constitution, one of which amends the constitution to include reference to the army and its commander, or who is to lead the army, and that's contained in amendment III.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then in amendment III we have the -- and does it also make reference to the fact that the president of the republic appoints, promotes, and discharges offices of the army of the Serbian Republic of BH in accordance with the law?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have exhibit -- Rule 65 ter 06733.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is -- is this the document that you referred to earlier when you said that they issued a decision on the formation of the army and appointed Mladic as commander?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was Mladic's position before he became commander of the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?
He was the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did he take that appointment, approximately?
That was at the end of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Rule 65 ter number 06605 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity on which appointment is this, the 2nd Military District or commander of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is appointment as commander of the new army of the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exhibit 190 is the -- is that, but Mr. Treanor referred to his prior position from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I wanted to know. Now, that date of April 1992, does it refer to the former job, or does it refer to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The former job, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your evidence, Mr. Treanor, that they adopted laws relating to the army and that was the law on the army and the law on the defence. What we see on the screen now is the law on the army, is it not? When was that, in fact -- when was that decision taken to implement that law?
The law on the army was passed on the -- I believe it was the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can take you to Article 174, which is on page 25 of the English translation and page 17 of the B/C/S. It states there in Article 174 that the supreme commander of the army is the president of the republic. Now, you told us a moment ago that on the 12th of May, they passed a law, a constitutional law amendment so that there could be a three-member Presidency with Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, and Radovan Karadzic.
Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So at that point they would be the supreme commander of the army; is that right?
Yes. The Presidency was exercising the powers of the president, so the Presidency was the commander-in-chief of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the same date, on the 1st of June, 1992, when they passed this law on the army, did they pass any other constitutional laws?
Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were they?

They passed another amendment to the constitutional law that again restructured the transitional office of the Presidency by providing that it be expanded from three to five members, under certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were the members of the extended Presidency?
Well, the members of this expanded Presidency would have been the three members of the Presidency, with the addition of the President of the Assembly and the President of the Government.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who were those persons?
Momcilo Krajisnik was the President of the Assembly and Branko Djeric was the President of the Government.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did that law say how long this extended Presidency -- or what were the conditions upon which the extended Presidency was to be set up?
The law stated that that was to apply during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in that law did it then say how long -- what was the duration that they were then to be acting as the president of the Serbian republic?
There was no temporal time limit put on. Just the condition of a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was Karadzic elected President of Republika Srpska?
Radovan Karadzic was elected President of Republika Srpska on the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I can just take you back, when did the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina turn into the Republika Srpska?
There were -- in August 1992, pursuant to further constitutional amendment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document that's on the screen, the law on the army, be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 06650 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I have exhibit number 06659 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this the decision that you were referring to on the 17th of December, 1992, electing Karadzic to -- as President of RS, Republika Srpska?
No. In the Serbian it's showing, but it's not showing in the English. In the Serbian it's showing at the top of the right-hand column.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we could use the second translation that's attached to the e-court for that Rule 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just for purposes of clarification, perhaps I'm a bit confused, the document that was previously discussed, that being the amendment to the constitution for which the witness indicated there was no time limit, is not a document that has been proffered at this point. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wasn't it P191?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure. That's why I'm -- I thought --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, that wasn't -- I didn't bring that document up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We just talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, the document that's now on the screen, is that the decision electing Karadzic as President?
Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I would now like to turn your attention to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You mentioned in the beginning of your testimony about the formation of a new Yugoslavia. When, in fact, was that formed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could have Rule 65 ter number 00441.01 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what happened on that date?
A constitution of the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, commonly known as the FRY, what was that to be composed of?
It was composed of the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention to Article number 2 of the constitution, could it be joined by other member republics?
We don't have the translation of that showing, and it's not in this binder. It could be joined by other entities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you know the article numbers in relation to who commands the army of the FRY, the article numbers of the constitution which --
Not off the top of my head. If I could look at the constitution from my Serbian binder, I'd be pleased to find that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could direct you to Article 135.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just finding the page number for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, Article 135, does that tell you who commanded the army?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what does it say?
Well, since I don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you still haven't given us the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sorry, the English translation has not been uploaded, and I apologise for that. It's only the cover page. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, who was the president of the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?
At this date the powers of the president of the new republic were being exercised by the Presidency of the SFRY until such time as a president of the FRY was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just can I interrupt? Just to make sure that the record is clear, by "move on," do you mean that you withdraw 00441.01?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At this stage, Your Honour, I don't seek to tender it because we don't have the translation in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to make sure that the record shows what fate it was. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, who was as elected as President of the FRY?
Dobrica Cosic was elected President of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the date?
He was elected on, I believe, the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the Supreme Defence Council. What is that body?

The Supreme Defence Council in the SFRY was a body established by the constitution of the SFRY in article 135. It was composed of the president of the republic and the presidents of the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the names of those persons?
The President of the Republic of Serbia at this time was Slobodan Milosevic, and at this time the President, or President of the Presidency, of Montenegro was Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Besides these people, who also attended Supreme Defence Council meetings?

The Supreme Defence Council meetings were attended by other high federal civilian and military officials, such as the prime minister or the president of the government, the minister of defence, the Chief of the general staff, sometimes other members of the general staff or other high military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the Chief of the General Staff at that time in mid-1992?
I believe the Chief of Staff at this time was Zivota Panic. I'm not sure when Zivota Panic came in. He replaced, I believe, General Adzic at around this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the minister for defence?

The Minister of Defence would have been -- well, I suppose initially the -- immediately after the 27th of April, until the formation of a new government, the minister or acting minister of the SFRY would have been acting defence minister, and that would have been Blagoje Adzic, until such time as he resigned which, as I say, was around this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the prime minister?

Again, until the formation of a new government in the summer after elections took place on the 31st of May, 1992, the acting prime minister would have been the prime minister or the acting prime minister of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was the SDC, the Supreme Defence Council, governed by any rules of procedure?
Yes. The SDC adopted rules of procedure at its third session, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately the date?
I believe that was in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did those rules of procedure set out how the SDC was to conduct its work?
Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what -- what was the process, the procedure, that had to be followed according to these rules in relation to its work at the sessions?
Well, it stated that it would carry out its work at the sessions on the basis of materials supplied to it by the federal -- by federal organs, such as the Ministry of Defence or the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was it to adopt -- how was it -- how did it arrive at its decision-making process? What was the decision-making process?
Well, they made decisions by consensus, and the president of the republic issued the appropriate -- the appropriate orders in his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We discussed earlier the strategic objectives that were announced at the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992. Was the FRY leadership aware of those strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Rule 65 ter number 06974 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 41 of the English translation and page 49 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is this document?
This is a transcript of an audiotape of the 2nd session of the Supreme Defence Council held on 8 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What draws you to the conclusion that the FRY leadership were aware of the strategic objectives enunciated by the Bosnian Serbs?

Well, they hold a discussion about military activities in the neighbourhood of Sarajevo, that is, Bosnian Serb military activities. They express their disapproval of those activities and suggest that -- they try to convince the Serbs in Bosnia to change their strategy -- to change their strategy, "to take the pressure off us."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does Dobrica Cosic say about that in particular?
He says at the bottom of page 42 -- is that what we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Page 41.
I'd spare the Court the beginning of the discussion on page 41 and just move to page 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's page 42 of the English translation and I think also 50 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the bottom of page 42, in the conclusion of this discussion, Dobrica Cosic says: "Momir, we all have work to do here to convince Serbs in Bosnia to change their strategy, to take this pressure off of us," and Momir being Momir Bulatovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then does Zivota Panic have anything to say on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could go to page 43 of the English translation and page 51 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, on page 43 of the translation, the second speaker on that page, Zivota Panic, I think to understand his remark it's best to refer to the remark made below it by Dobrica Cosic, so I'll read both. Zivota Panic says: "They made a strategy plan, and they're going to realise it." Dobrica Cosic says: "I feeling that everything developed according to a strategic programme. Every concession we make triggers the next step of theirs towards the achievement of the main aim, the main aim being obviously breaking this area and this country that we're trying to establish." The "they" being referring to are the opponents of the Bosnian Serbs and the strategic plan that Dobrica Cosic is alluding to is -- would be their plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, if you may just refresh my memory, in the decision on the admission of Mr. Treanor's report, did the decision not deny admission of the summaries of the minutes on the basis, amongst others, that the Chamber can read those minutes? It's just a compilation of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I wrong to surmise that this is a record of the minutes, a transcription, he called it, a transcription of the audio-recording of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're right. You're correct, it is a transcript of the 2nd session; however, this is referred to in Mr. Treanor's report. He refers to eight or so sessions of the SDC minutes, or transcripts, in his Belgrade report that has been -- that he has been allowed to testify about, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we are in the midst of a break, as I understand it, these are the transcript notes of an audio-tape, and we do not have a copy of that audio-tape. And I would ask at this point, depending on where there's going, that this document be MFIed until we can deal with issues of authenticity and other issues, and I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. The Prosecution does not have an audio of these transcripts either. These were provided to us by the Serbian government, the transcripts and the minutes, but we were not provided with audios.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Very well. I'll leave it at that for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. On that "uh-huh" note, we'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence, in particular the pages that we have referred to during Mr. Treanor's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. It looks like there are lots of pages. The pages of 65 ter 06974 that have been referred to are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those pages would be Exhibit P193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Rule 65 ter number 06669 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, do you know of any other example where the FRY leadership were aware or made reference to the strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think that mischaracterises, in fact, the testimony thus far. The pages just read and the testimony just given talk about a strategy which is open to interpretation based upon the information contained therein. The question is also leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't agree, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please, you may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we said to the last objection, the Defence are able to cross-examine Mr. Treanor about this. My earlier question to him was, Were you aware of any strategic -- the FRY leadership being aware of the strategy objectives. He said yes. I took him to one document. My next question was: Are you aware of any other examples where the strategic objectives were mentioned by the FRY leadership, the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: See, the distinction is -- the distinction between strategic objectives and strategic goals is strategic goals have obtained a -- are almost a term of art here. As I was reviewing the previous documents, it's clear that there's a discussion about a strategy, and it's clear that that strategy may well be involved with issues concerning Sarajevo. Whether or not that in and of itself defines the SDC's awareness of the strategic goals, as the Prosecution suggests, is a different matter. Now, if the Prosecution wish to ask about the matter of strategy or strategic objectives, because initially -- and I did not object earlier because issues of objection as opposed to goals, I consider there to be a distinction, perhaps a distinction without a difference to the Prosecution. But quite frankly, among -- well, the objection is for two reasons. I think, first of all, I maintain it mischaracterises the previous testimony, and second of all, it's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think I now understand what you're saying. Let me just make sure I do. By "mischaracterisation," you are saying strategic goals are now being cast as strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. That's a simple one to resolve. I. Thought Mr. Treanor is testifying here as an expert and not an ordinary witness. Therefore, questions of leading would not be that very relevant because, in fact, he testifies with his report in front of him to refresh his memory. The essence is going to come when he gives this Court his professional opinion based on all that we are going through here.
